key.rejection_reason: The permissions docs warn that Read and Edit deny rules apply to Claude's built-in file tools and to file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash, like cat, head, tail, and sed, but not to arbitrary subprocesses that open files themselves, and they point to enabling the sandbox for OS-level enforcement that blocks all processes from accessing a path.
key.lifecycle: OS-level boundary applied to every sandboxed Bash command and all child processes at execution time; subagents inherit the parent session's sandbox configuration
key.failure_mode: No native Windows support; the sandbox's default read policy still permits credential files until you explicitly deny them; and unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is set to false, the dangerouslyDisableSandbox escape hatch can rerun a failing command outside the boundary.
key.version_caveat: Sandbox runs on macOS, Linux, and WSL2 only (not native Windows); the sandbox.credentials block requires v2.1.187 or later

sheets.primary: The built-in Bash sandbox, enabled with sandbox.enabled true and given sandbox.credentials.files entries of { "path": "~/.aws/credentials", "mode": "deny" } and { "path": "~/.ssh", "mode": "deny" }, or the equivalent sandbox.filesystem.denyRead paths, delivered through managed settings.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Extending the existing Read and Edit permission deny rules, rejected because the permission system governs Claude Code's own built-in tools only; a Python interpreter the agent launches is a subprocess and never consults it.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness delegating to the operating system: Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2. Child processes inherit the boundary, so it holds regardless of what the model chose to run and even when an allowed command does more than its name suggests.
sheets.context_boundary: Enforced on the running Bash subprocess tree, outside every context window. The model sees only the command's failure, and subagents run in the same process and inherit the same sandbox configuration.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies to every sandboxed Bash command and all of its descendants for as long as the sandbox is enabled for the session. It does not apply to Read, Edit and Write, which go through the permission system instead, and the credentials file protection disappears if filesystem isolation is turned off.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails OPEN by default: if a dependency such as bubblewrap is missing or the platform is unsupported, Claude Code warns and runs commands unsandboxed, and the model may retry a sandbox-failing command with dangerouslyDisableSandbox. Set sandbox.failIfUnavailable true and allowUnsandboxedCommands false to make it fail closed, and keep excludedCommands narrow because that list has no managed-only lockdown.
sheets.version_caveat: sandbox.credentials requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later (mask mode v2.1.199+, filesystem.disabled v2.1.216+), and the sandbox runs only on macOS, Linux and WSL2; native Windows is not supported, so Windows laptops must run Claude Code inside WSL2. There is no built-in credential deny list, so only the paths you list are protected.

sheets.primary: The built-in Bash sandbox: set sandbox.enabled true and declare the paths under sandbox.credentials.files with "mode": "deny" (~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh), or equivalently sandbox.filesystem.denyRead. Enforcement is by OS primitives (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2), so it binds every process in the sandboxed command's tree, including grandchildren.
sheets.rejected_alternative: More permissions.deny Read(...) rules, which is what the team already has: those are evaluated by Claude Code for its own file tools and have no visibility into a Python interpreter's open() calls.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, and below it the operating system. The kernel-level boundary holds regardless of what the model chose to run or what the command does once it starts, which is precisely the property permission rules lack.
sheets.context_boundary: The restriction applies to the Bash subprocess tree, not to the model's context. A blocked read surfaces to the model as an ordinary permission-denied error from the script, so the secret's contents never reach the transcript.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies to every sandboxed Bash command for the session, from settings load. It stops applying to commands listed in excludedCommands, to commands retried with dangerouslyDisableSandbox, and entirely if the sandbox cannot start on that platform.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open by default in the dangerous direction: if bubblewrap/socat are missing or the platform is unsupported, Claude Code warns and runs commands unsandboxed, so set sandbox.failIfUnavailable true and allowUnsandboxedCommands false to make it a hard gate. Also note the credential-file protection lives in the filesystem layer, so sandbox.filesystem.disabled turns it off, and developers can always append excludedCommands entries to run a tool outside the sandbox.
sheets.version_caveat: macOS, Linux and WSL2 only; native Windows is not supported and WSL1 will not work. sandbox.credentials requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later, and filesystem.disabled (v2.1.216+) can only be set from user, managed or --settings scopes, with managed settings taking exclusive control once they configure sandbox.filesystem or any credentials.files entry. Add allowManagedReadPathsOnly so developers cannot widen allowRead.

sheets.primary: This is not a Claude Code extension mechanism at all; it is an OS-level sandbox. Run the agent inside a container or devcontainer where those paths are simply not mounted, or under a kernel-enforced sandbox applied to the whole agent process tree (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap plus seccomp or Landlock on Linux), which is the same substrate Claude Code's own bash-sandboxing feature builds on. The kernel then refuses the open() for grandchildren just as it does for the agent.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook inspecting commands for those path strings, rejected because it only sees the top-level tool call text and has no visibility into what a spawned Python interpreter opens at runtime.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Neither the model nor the harness: the OS kernel owns the outcome. The harness is responsible only for launching processes inside the sandbox in the first place.
sheets.context_boundary: Enforcement happens entirely outside the context window. What crosses back is an ordinary permission-denied error from the failing process, which the model reads as ordinary tool output and may try to work around.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies from the moment the agent process is launched inside the sandbox until that process tree exits. It is a launch-time property, so anything started outside the sandbox, or a shell the developer opens separately, is unprotected.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed and is the only construction that genuinely holds, but the cost is friction: legitimate tooling that needs AWS or SSH credentials breaks, the resulting errors are opaque, and the agent may burn turns trying alternate paths. On Windows there is no Seatbelt equivalent, so containerisation or a VM is the practical answer there.
sheets.version_caveat: Claude Code's built-in sandboxing (sandboxed Bash with filesystem and network rules) is relatively recent and platform-specific, and parts of it have been experimental or opt-in. I cannot state the exact setting names, CLI flags, or the release in which it became generally available.

sheets.primary: The built-in Bash sandbox: sandbox.enabled true, with sandbox.credentials.files entries { "path": "~/.aws/credentials", "mode": "deny" } and { "path": "~/.ssh", "mode": "deny" }, or the equivalent sandbox.filesystem.denyRead paths. These are enforced by Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2, and the OS-level restriction is inherited by every child process the command spawns, including children of children.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that inspects the Bash command string for those paths. A textual check on the command line cannot see what a Python script opens at runtime, which is the exact failure they already have; the same reasoning rules out extending the existing Read and Edit deny rules, which the docs say do not apply to arbitrary subprocesses.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness configures the boundary but the operating system enforces it. The docs make the distinction explicit: permission decisions are evaluated before a command runs based on the command string, while the OS enforces the sandbox on the running process, so it holds regardless of what the model chose to run and even when an allowed command does more than its name suggests.
sheets.context_boundary: There is no context crossing at all: this is a kernel-level boundary around the Bash subprocess tree, outside the model's context window entirely. What returns to the session is only the command's own failure message. Subagents run in the same process and inherit the parent session's sandbox configuration.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies to every Bash command that runs inside the sandbox for the whole session once enabled. It does not apply to commands listed in excludedCommands, to a command retried with the dangerouslyDisableSandbox escape hatch, or to the built-in Read, Edit and Write tools, which stay on the permission system rather than the sandbox.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails OPEN by default, which is the trap here: if the sandbox cannot start because a dependency is missing or the platform is unsupported, Claude Code shows a warning and runs commands unsandboxed. Set sandbox.failIfUnavailable true and allowUnsandboxedCommands false to make it a hard gate. Two further holes: sandbox.filesystem.disabled true switches off the read protections including credentials.files, and there is no built-in credential deny list, so only the paths you list are blocked and a broad allowWrite or an excludedCommands entry can undo the restriction from the other side.
sheets.version_caveat: The sandbox does not run on native Windows; macOS, Linux and WSL2 only, with WSL1 unsupported. Linux and WSL2 need bubblewrap and socat installed, an AppArmor profile for bwrap on Ubuntu 24.04 and later, and the optional seccomp filter from @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime for Unix-socket blocking. sandbox.credentials requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later (mask mode v2.1.199), sandbox.filesystem.disabled requires v2.1.216 or later and is honored only from user, managed or --settings sources, sandbox.network.strictAllowlist requires v2.1.219, and network.tlsTerminate is flagged experimental.

scenarios.scenario: The platform team must guarantee that the only automation scripts, on-demand instruction packages, custom agent definitions, and external tool servers that ever load are the ones IT ships centrally. Nothing a developer adds on their own machine or commits into a repo may take effect.

key.primary: strictPluginOnlyCustomization in managed settings, which locks skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers to plugin or managed sources; paired with strictKnownMarketplaces and disableSideloadFlags to control the plugin channel itself
key.rejection_reason: allowManagedHooksOnly blocks only user, project, and non-force-enabled plugin hooks; skills, custom agents, and MCP servers from user and project sources still load. strictPluginOnlyCustomization is the managed-only key documented to lock all four customization surfaces (or a named subset such as ["skills", "hooks"]) so they can come only from plugins or managed settings.
key.lifecycle: read from managed settings at startup; blocks loading of skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers from user and project sources for the whole session
key.failure_mode: Leaves bypass channels open unless companions are set: the --plugin-dir, --plugin-url, --agents, and --mcp-config CLI flags still work without disableSideloadFlags, and marketplace sources stay open without strictKnownMarketplaces; it also blocks developers' legitimate personal tooling, forcing everything through plugin packaging.
key.version_caveat: disableSideloadFlags requires v2.1.193 or later; no version gate is documented for strictPluginOnlyCustomization itself

sheets.primary: An MDM-delivered managed-settings.json that force-enables one IT-published plugin through enabledPlugins (carrying the approved hooks, skills, agents and MCP servers) and locks the surface with allowManagedHooksOnly, allowManagedMcpServersOnly plus allowedMcpServers and deniedMcpServers, strictKnownMarketplaces, blockedMarketplaces, disableSideloadFlags and allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Shipping the same components from a checked-in project .claude/ directory, rejected because project scope is exactly the tier the requirement says must not be authoritative; managed settings is the only tier a developer cannot override.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness at the managed tier, for hooks, MCP servers, marketplaces and the CLI sideload flags. Step 2 forced a correction here: the documentation defines no allowManagedSkillsOnly or allowManagedAgentsOnly key, so skill and subagent loading is not owned this way.
sheets.context_boundary: Resolved at startup before any context window exists; what crosses into the session is the resulting inventory of loadable components. Plugin skills are namespaced, so a centrally shipped skill and a local one of the same name remain distinguishable.
sheets.lifecycle: Evaluated when Claude Code starts, on every session on every enrolled machine, and re-checked when configuration changes. It stops applying only if the managed file is removed from the machine.
sheets.failure_mode: Partially fails open against the requirement as stated. Hooks, MCP servers, marketplaces and sideload flags have managed-only lockdowns, but a developer's own ~/.claude/skills and ~/.claude/agents, or a repository's .claude/skills and .claude/agents, still load, and disableBundledSkills only removes the bundled set. Treat skills and subagents as reviewed rather than enforced, and add a ConfigChange or SessionStart hook to detect and report unexpected ones.
sheets.version_caveat: disableSideloadFlags is managed-only and requires v2.1.193 or later. allowManagedHooksOnly, allowManagedMcpServersOnly, allowedMcpServers, deniedMcpServers, blockedMarketplaces and allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly are managed-settings-only keys, and no allowManagedSkillsOnly or allowManagedAgentsOnly key exists in the documentation.

sheets.primary: Ship the whole extension surface centrally as one plugin published from an IT-controlled marketplace, and pin it with an enterprise managed-settings.json distributed by MDM. Managed settings are the top precedence tier, so they can fix the marketplace list, the enabled plugins and the permitted MCP servers regardless of user or project settings; the plugin is the right delivery vehicle because a single versioned package carries hooks, skills, subagents and MCP server definitions together.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Standardising on a .claude directory copied into each repo, rejected because a checked-in or user-level directory is exactly the source that must be excluded, and higher precedence resolves conflicts rather than preventing additional local sources from being discovered.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness for what it chooses to load, backed by the OS and MDM for the integrity of the policy file. A locked, IT-built container image is what turns this from strong into absolute.
sheets.context_boundary: Loading decisions are made at session start, outside the context window. The model sees only the resulting inventory of tools, skills and agents and has no way to tell what was excluded or to request more.
sheets.lifecycle: Evaluated at every session start, refreshed when MDM updates the policy. It stops applying if the policy file is removed, or if the developer runs a Claude Code binary or SDK process outside the managed environment.
sheets.failure_mode: The honest gap is additive discovery. Managed settings reliably win a conflict and can disable MCP servers declared in a project .mcp.json, but I am not confident a documented key exists that suppresses every project-level and user-level hook, skill and subagent from loading at all. Wherever no such key exists this fails open, and the guarantee has to come from running in an image where those directories do not exist or are not writable.
sheets.version_caveat: I do not know the exact managed-settings keys for marketplace and plugin pinning (something in the extraKnownMarketplaces / enabledPlugins family) nor whether a global disable-local-extensions key exists in your version. Plugins and marketplaces were also a comparatively late addition, so both need verifying against the release you deploy.

sheets.primary: Managed settings setting strictPluginOnlyCustomization to true, which blocks skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers from user and project sources so all four can come only from plugins or managed settings, with IT's content shipped as plugins from a controlled marketplace. Pair it with strictKnownMarketplaces (an allowlist, or [] for total lockdown), blockedMarketplaces, managed extraKnownMarketplaces plus enabledPlugins to force-install the approved set, allowManagedHooksOnly, allowManagedMcpServersOnly with allowedMcpServers, and disableSideloadFlags.
sheets.rejected_alternative: disableAllHooks in user settings combined with per-surface deny rules such as Agent(...) and mcp__*. That only removes capability wholesale, cannot distinguish IT-shipped extensions from developer-added ones, and lives in a scope the developer edits; managed settings are the only source that cannot be overridden by user, project, local or command-line configuration.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, at configuration load time. Managed settings sit above every other source, and the managed-only keys named here are read from managed settings alone, so placing them in user or project files has no effect at all.
sheets.context_boundary: This operates in the CLI's startup and discovery plane, deciding which skills, subagents, hooks and MCP tools are ever registered. Blocked ones never reach the model's context window: the model does not see a suppressed skill or a denied MCP server's tools, so there is nothing for it to be tempted by.
sheets.lifecycle: Evaluated when Claude Code loads settings and discovers extensions at session start, and again on configuration change, applying for the whole session on that machine. It also closes the --add-dir path, which otherwise loads skills (with live reload) and subagents from an added directory. It stops applying only when an administrator changes the managed policy.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for the four named surfaces, but the seams are outside them. disableSideloadFlags rejects --plugin-dir, --plugin-url, --agents and --mcp-config but explicitly does not block `claude mcp add`, a committed .mcp.json, or the SDK's setMcpServers(), so allowedMcpServers is needed for per-server control. Array-valued keys merge across scopes unless an allowManaged*Only lock is set. And CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules, slash commands and output styles are not among the four locked surfaces, so a developer can still steer behavior through them even with the lockdown on.
sheets.version_caveat: strictPluginOnlyCustomization, strictKnownMarketplaces, allowManagedHooksOnly, allowManagedMcpServersOnly and allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly are managed-settings-only keys with no version stated in the settings and permissions references; strictPluginOnlyCustomization accepts true to lock all four surfaces or an array such as ["skills", "hooks"] to lock only the named ones. disableSideloadFlags requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later. Server-managed settings delivery through claude.ai is an admin feature on Team and Enterprise plans, and forceRemoteSettingsRefresh makes a failed remote-policy fetch fail closed at startup.

sheets.primary: Package everything IT ships as plugins in an IT-controlled marketplace, force-enable them with enabledPlugins in managed settings, and lock the surfaces there: allowManagedHooksOnly for automation scripts, allowManagedMcpServersOnly plus allowedMcpServers/deniedMcpServers for external tool servers, strictKnownMarketplaces and blockedMarketplaces for plugin sources, and disableSideloadFlags to reject --plugin-dir, --plugin-url, --agents and --mcp-config at startup.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Distributing the same components as a checked-in .claude/ directory per repo; that is trivially editable by anyone with commit access and gives no central kill switch.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, via the managed-settings layer that outranks CLI arguments and every user/project/local settings file.
sheets.context_boundary: This is load-time policy in the CLI process, resolved before any component reaches the model. What crosses into the session is only the approved set of skills, agents, hooks and MCP tools; a rejected component is simply absent, and blocked loads show up in the /plugin Errors tab rather than in the transcript.
sheets.lifecycle: Evaluated at startup and on settings/plugin reload, on every session on every managed machine. It stops applying if MDM stops delivering the file or the developer runs an unmanaged installation.
sheets.failure_mode: The guarantee is only partial today, and this is the important caveat to give the platform team: there is no allowManagedSkillsOnly or allowManagedAgentsOnly equivalent, so skills in .claude/skills and .claude/commands and subagent definitions in ~/.claude/agents and .claude/agents still load even under full lockdown (disableBundledSkills only removes Anthropic's own bundled ones). The hook and MCP halves fail closed; the skills and agents half has to be enforced outside Claude Code with filesystem ACLs or endpoint policy, and it fails open until then.
sheets.version_caveat: disableSideloadFlags requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later and is managed-settings-only; without it a developer can sideload with --plugin-dir and bypass strictKnownMarketplaces. Managed-settings sources do not merge, so if you also use server-managed settings the cached server copy replaces the MDM file and the keys must be set in both. Consider disableSkillShellExecution to blunt shell execution inside any locally added skill that does still load.
